title: The Expedition of Mu'tah
subtitle: The Northern Frontier, the Slain Emissary, and the Appointment of the Three Commanders
summary: In Jumada al-Ula of the eighth year after the Hijrah, the Prophet mobilized three thousand warriors toward southern Syria following the egregious murder of his diplomatic emissary, Al-Harith ibn Umayr al-Azdi. In an unprecedented prophetic command recorded in authentic Hadith, the succession of three commanders—Zayd ibn Harithah, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, and Abdullah ibn Rawahah—was established before the army marched north into modern Jordan to confront a massive Byzantine coalition.

sections.text: Diplomatic Murder on the Syrian Frontier

Following the stabilization of central Arabia and the signing of the Hudaybiyyah pact, the Prophet dispatched letters to regional monarchs and tribal rulers across the Near East, inviting them to monotheism and universal justice. Among these diplomatic couriers was Al-Harith ibn Umayr al-Azdi, who was dispatched with a message addressed to the Byzantine vassal ruler of Busra in southern Syria. While traversing the border district of Mut'ah in the region of Al-Balqa (modern-day Jordan), Al-Harith was ambushed, arrested, and brutally executed by Shurahbil ibn Amr al-Ghassani, a local chieftain allied with the Roman Empire.

The murder of an accredited diplomatic envoy was an outrage that no sovereign entity could overlook without forfeiting its security and credibility. Never before had an emissary of the Prophet been harmed while carrying a message. Recognizing that this provocative act signaled an aggressive hostile posture along the northern frontier, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered immediate military mobilization in Madinah to establish deterrence and secure the northern trade routes.
The Assembly of Three Thousand and the Succession of Command

In Jumada al-Ula of 8 AH, an army of three thousand warriors gathered at the staging area of Jurf outside Madinah—the largest expeditionary force the Muslim state had ever dispatched beyond the borders of the Hijaz. As the army prepared to march, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood before them and delivered an extraordinary, prophetic command establishing a preordained succession of leadership:

أَمِيرُ النَّاسِ زَيْدُ بْنُ حَارِثَةَ، فَإِنْ قُتِلَ فَجَعْفَرٌ، فَإِنْ قُتِلَ فَابْنُ رَوَاحَةَ
'The commander of the people is Zayd ibn Harithah; if he is killed, then Ja'far; and if he is killed, then Ibn Rawahah.' (Sahih al-Bukhari 4261)

The companions listening to this decree were struck by its solemnity. The explicit naming of three successive commanders, conditioned upon each one's demise, carried an unmistakable premonition that these beloved leaders were marching toward their martyrdom. Among the army marched Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had embraced Islam only months prior and was participating as an ordinary volunteer in the ranks.
The March to Ma'an and the Reality of the Enemy

The army marched north through the arid wastes of Wadi al-Qura until they reached the town of Ma'an in southern Transjordan. There, scouting patrols gathered alarming intelligence: the Roman Emperor Heraclius had mobilized an enormous imperial army stationed at Ma'ab in the Balqa, reinforced by Christian Arab tribal levies from Lakhm, Judham, and Ghassan. Classical historical traditions record vast numbers—ranging up to one hundred thousand or two hundred thousand—for the combined Byzantine coalition, while modern academic historians view these figures as literary representations of a massively superior conventional force.

Confronted with such overwhelming disparity, the Muslim commanders held a war council in Ma'an, remaining there for two nights debating their strategic options. Some suggested sending a courier back to Madinah to inform the Prophet of the enemy's unexpected strength and await either reinforcements or new instructions.
The Inspiring Resolve of Abdullah ibn Rawahah
Sensing hesitation, the third commander, Abdullah ibn Rawahah, stood up and delivered an impassioned address that dissolved all doubt and rekindled the army's spirit:

يَا قَوْمِ، وَاللَّهِ إِنَّ الَّذِي تَكْرَهُونَ لَلَّذِي خَرَجْتُمْ تَطْلُبُونَ: الشَّهَادَةَ! وَمَا نُقَاتِلُ النَّاسَ بِعَدَدٍ وَلاَ قُوَّةٍ وَلاَ كَثْرَةٍ، مَا نُقَاتِلُهُمْ إِلاَّ بِهَذَا الدِّينِ الَّذِي أَكْرَمَنَا اللَّهُ بِهِ؛ فَانْطَلِقُوا فَإِنَّمَا هِيَ إِحْدَى الْحُسْنَيَيْنِ: إِمَّا ظُهُورٌ وَإِمَّا شَهَادَةٌ
'O people! By Allah, that which you dread is the very thing you departed seeking: martyrdom! We do not fight the enemy with numbers, nor with weapons, nor with vastness of strength; we fight them only with this religion with which Allah has honored us! March forward, for it is certainly one of the two glorious outcomes: either victory or martyrdom!' (Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah by Ibn Hisham)

Rallied by this stirring affirmation of faith, the army shouted in unison: 'By Allah, Ibn Rawahah has spoken the truth!' Breaking camp from Ma'an, the three thousand moved boldly northward toward the village of Mu'tah, prepared to encounter the imperial legions of Rome in an epic defense of diplomatic principle and monotheistic conviction.
